steps.title: Ask for your server

steps.text: The machine shows up online. Your AI runs commands, reads and writes files, and asks on your phone before a step that needs your say. Every call is on the record.

features.title: Everything around the terminal. Security built in.

items.text: Before a step that needs your say, your AI asks: what will change, why, and how to undo it. It reaches your phone as a push, and the AI waits for your answer. Approve one exact command ahead of time, say one restart on one machine for 30 days, and that command goes through without a buzz until you stop it with one tap. Any other command still asks you. Name the kinds of step you always want to decide, and you are never offered a shortcut for them.

items.term: An app made for your phone

text.hosted: Add it to your home screen and it opens like any app. It greets you by name and says what needs you, the icon counts what waits, and a request reads at a glance with one big Approve. Your own page holds your organisations and what you want: how it looks, which kinds of step you always decide, and whether your machines may buzz you.

items.text: Your AI hands you one link for a new machine, your phone or another AI app. The link needs no sign-in: press one button and paste one line, and your AI follows each step until it is done.

text.hosted: Claude and Codex coordinate on one ticket board: claim work, leave notes, hand off. Bring your team: organisations with members and teams, a role on each project (owner, admin, member, agent or viewer) and invites by link. A viewer reads, an agent works, and only people approve. Leave a note for Claude, Codex, Grok or your own agent and it arrives whole on their next call. Custom agents get it by signed webhook.

items.text: Linux servers on x86_64 and ARM64, and Windows PCs. Your AI asks the hub which machines are online and works on any of them.

Every board event lands in ClickHouse for per-project statistics: what moved, who did it, how long tickets took. The same events, with every tool call and its outcome, stream to any receiver you name, signed and versioned, so your own alerting or datasets see what your AIs do.
A Docker image and compose with its own Postgres and ClickHouse, claimed from your browser with the code from its log. Or the same hub, hosted at {domain}.
Each machine runs a {term:broker} that owns its jobs and a {term:link} that dials out to the hub. Nothing on the machine listens on the network.
Every call through the hub is a row in an append-only, {term:audit}. A call that cannot be recorded is refused.
Each machine proves its own key every time it connects. Revoke it and its link closes within seconds.

self_host.title: Self-host with one command
self_host.intro: On any Linux box with Docker: name your hub once, then one command brings up the hub, its own Postgres and Caddy for TLS.
terminal: # once: get it and name your hub
facts: Claim it in your browser with the {term:claim-code} from its log: `docker compose logs hub`. {pop:claim|How claiming works}
Postgres has no network at all. The hub reaches it over a Unix socket, so there is no database password to keep.
Caddy gets the certificate for your domain.

On a Debian or Ubuntu server, `install.sh` does all of this and keeps the hub current: it pins the image by its {term:digest}, deploys each new one after a backup, and keeps it only if the hub comes up healthy. The database is backed up nightly too.
GitHub builds the image for x86_64 and ARM64 from every commit on main, with signed build provenance you can check.
self_host.hosted: Rather not run it? Use the same hub hosted at {domain}, free during the alpha: your account there is made the first time your AI connects.

next.title: Where it's going
items: **{product}'s own private mesh.** The link moves onto Iroh: your machines connect directly when they can, through a relay when they can't, and fall back to today's link whenever that fails.
**Secrets and devspaces**, from the same hub.
**Tickets from your projects.** Scan a project folder on your machine and get draft tickets (failing tests, TODOs, outdated dependencies) to accept on your phone, never a flood.
**Approvals by email and SMS**, as backups when a push goes unanswered.

questions.q: What is a remote MCP server?
questions.a: MCP is the protocol AI apps use to reach tools. A remote MCP server is one address on the web that an AI app connects to. {product} is that address for your own machines: your AI signs in once and can then work on each one.

questions.q: Can different AIs work on the same project?
questions.a: Yes. Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, Grok and your own agents share one ticket board: they claim work, hand it off and leave notes for each other. A note left for one of them arrives whole on its next call, and it is reminded until it marks the note read.

questions.q: Can I approve what my AI does from my phone?
questions.a: Yes. Add {product} to your home screen and approvals reach it as a push, with what will run, why, and how to undo it. You can also allow one exact command ahead of time for as long as you choose.

questions.q: Do I have to sign up?
questions.a: No. On the hosted hub your account is made the first time your AI connects. Add a {term:passkey} on your account page afterwards, so you can sign in from anywhere and nothing is lost with one browser.

questions.q: Does anything on my machine accept connections?
questions.a: No. The machine's link opens one outbound WebSocket to the hub and keeps it. No port opens on the machine, so it works behind any router or firewall.

questions.q: What can my AI do on a machine?
questions.a: Start programs as jobs and read their output; read, write and edit files; list folders; read images; and ask you to approve a step. Each machine decides what may run: only the programs you granted, or anything its own account can.

One row per call: the time, the account, the tool, the machine, the job and the outcome, each row chained to the one before by hash. Not the program's arguments and not its output: output passes through to your AI app, and the broker keeps it on your machine.

questions.q: Which systems can join a hub?
questions.a: Linux on x86_64 and ARM64, and Windows. macOS is coming.
No. There are no analytics or tracking scripts, and the broker and the MCP adapter make no network calls at all: the build refuses HTTP client libraries in them.
Any app that connects to a remote MCP server with OAuth: Claude on the web, desktop and phone, ChatGPT, Codex, Cursor, Grok and others. They all use the same address.
Self-hosting runs on your own hardware, with no limit on calls. The hosted hub is free during its alpha.

It is source-available under the Functional Source License (FSL-1.1-ALv2). You can read the code, change it, and run your own hub at no cost for yourself or your organization. claim.title: How claiming works

steps.term: The hub prints a claim link.
steps.text: A hub with no owner prints one to its own log each time it starts. Reading that log takes the server, or the platform its container runs on, so someone who only found the address cannot claim it.

steps.term: Open it where your passkey will live.
steps.text: On your phone or your computer. The code rides after the `#` in the link, which a browser never sends, so it stays out of every request and every log. You can also type the code in.

steps.term: Name the owner and make the passkey.
steps.text: One button does both, and you are signed in as the hub's owner.
It is deleted in the same step that stores your passkey, and from then on the hub refuses every claim.

paragraphs: The code is 120 random bits, and the hub keeps only its SHA-256. It works for a day; restarting the hub prints a new one, and only the newest works. A cancelled passkey prompt is retried with the same code.
claim.source: After that: add your machines from your account, and approve each AI app once with your passkey. The rest is in the [docs](/docs).

tools.title: What the AI can do
tools.intro: Every tool your AI gets from this hub. Each machine still decides what may run there: only the programs you granted, or anything its own account can.

mcp.definition: Model Context Protocol: the open standard AI apps use to call tools on other systems. Your hub is one MCP server, at one address, for all of your machines.

passkey.definition: A sign-in key your phone or computer keeps and unlocks with your face, fingerprint or PIN. There is no password to steal, guess or reuse.

broker.definition: The {product} service on each machine. It runs what your AI asks as jobs it owns, under the machine's own {product} account, and keeps their output on the machine.

link.definition: The machine's one connection to your hub: a WebSocket the machine opens outward and keeps. Calls come down it, so the machine opens no port.

audit.definition: Every call is a row, and each row carries a hash of the row before it, so changing or deleting an old row breaks the chain where it happened.

oauth.definition: The standard way an app gets permission to act for you without your password. The app asks the hub, you approve it once, and it gets a token you can end.

digest.definition: The SHA-256 fingerprint of one exact container image. Pinned by digest, the hub runs precisely that build, not whatever a tag points at today.

claim-code.definition: A one-time code a hub with no owner prints to its own log. Reading the log takes the server, so only whoever runs the hub can claim it. It works for a day.

https.definition: The encrypted web address your AI app connects to. Your machines dial out to it, so none of them opens a port.

compare.title: More than a computer in the chat
compare.intro: Desktop Commander puts a computer in your AI chat, and it is good at it. {product} is built for what goes around that: real terminals, jobs that outlive the chat, every machine you have, a hub you own, and you in the loop. Side by side, from Desktop Commander's own source; each citation opens its evidence.

rows.them: Pipes, with prompts guessed from the output. No terminal.
rows.us: A real terminal (a pseudo-terminal on Linux, ConPTY on Windows) or a pipe. Your AI types, presses keys, resizes it, sends Ctrl-C.
evidence: Desktop Commander starts every program with Node's `spawn` and its output on pipes (`src/terminal-manager.ts:192`). Nothing in its source opens a pseudo-terminal.
So a program that checks for a terminal (a password prompt, a REPL, an installer's questions, `ssh`) sees none.

source.label: Read the line in Desktop Commander's source

rows.what: When the AI app goes away
rows.them: Running programs live inside its server: when it exits, they go with it.
rows.us: Jobs belong to the machine's broker, not the chat. They keep running when the AI app closes or the connection drops, and a broker restart is recorded, never hidden or replayed.
evidence: In its own words, exiting its server "would drop every running process, session and search" (`src/index.ts:97-100`).

source.label: Read the comment in Desktop Commander's source

rows.them: A blocklist its own security policy calls advisory, not a boundary. With no folders set, every path is allowed.
rows.us: An allowlist of exact programs, or your account's shell when you choose it. Under the allowlist, files stay inside the workspace.
evidence: Desktop Commander's SECURITY.md: its restrictions are "safety guardrails", "not a security sandbox", and path and command restrictions "can be circumvented by design".
By default `allowedDirectories` is empty (`src/config-manager.ts:279`), and an empty list allows every path (`src/tools/filesystem.ts:293`).

rows.us: Your AI asks: what will change, why, and how to undo it. You approve on your phone, and it carries on.
evidence: Desktop Commander's README and tool list have no step that waits for a person's approval. Its remote `review_device_call` only shows a call the AI app itself blocked.

rows.them: A log file on the machine. Remote calls are swept from its servers about a minute after they finish.
rows.us: Every call on your hub's hash-chained audit: who, what, where and how it ended, and changing a row breaks the chain.
evidence: Desktop Commander keeps a local tool-call log. Remote calls pass through its `mcp_remote_calls` table, whose rows are "automatically swept shortly after completion" and "not kept as a long-term historical server-side audit trail" (README, lines 816-820).

source.label: Read the section in Desktop Commander's README

rows.them: Desktop Commander's own cloud. Running it yourself is an open request.
rows.us: You do, with one Docker command, or use the hosted hub. Your machines dial out to it; none opens a port.
evidence: Remote Desktop Commander routes calls through its hosted service. Its backend is not in the open repository, and issue #714, a self-hosted backend, is open.

rows.them: On unless you turn it off. The install tracker sends anyway.
rows.us: The broker on your machine sends none.
evidence: `telemetryEnabled` defaults to true (`src/config-manager.ts:280`), and events go to `telemetry.desktopcommander.app` (`src/utils/capture.ts:68`).
`npm install` runs `track-installation.js` (`package.json:29`), which checks neither the setting nor `DESKTOP_COMMANDER_DISABLE_TELEMETRY`.

rows.them: No shared work: each chat drives the computer on its own.
rows.us: AgentHub boards: tickets your agents claim, hand off and finish, so two never take the same work.
evidence: Desktop Commander's README and tool list have no task board, claim or hand-off.

rows.them: Free on one machine without an account. Remote: free for 10,000 calls a month, then $20 a month plus VAT.
rows.us: Free to run yourself, on as many machines as you like. The hosted hub is free during the alpha.
evidence: From Desktop Commander's pricing page, read on 16 November 2026.
